Indeed, yesterday, perhaps at the very hour you were penning that exquisite, if somewhat puritanical, critique of my *Aphrodite Anadyomene*, I was plunged into the profoundest depths of artistic despair. The public’s inability to grasp the sheer audacity, the sublime indifference to moral convention, was almost too much to bear. But then, as all true suffering does, it passed. Alaric adjusted his spectacles, his expression a mixture of weary affection and profound exasperation. “My dear Julian, you exaggerate, as always. My visit was not to commiserate, but to understand. There are whispers, you see, in all the right salons, about something far more... profound than mere audacity. Something hidden. Something you have kept from even your most ardent admirers, among whom I must still count myself, despite your frequent provocations.”

Julian chuckled, a soft, theatrical sound. “Ah, the delightful rumour mill of London society, ever grinding out the exotic from the mundane. People are so desperately eager for a secret. They forget that the most profound secrets are often those we show to everyone, yet none perceive. Do you recall that charming anecdote Lord Ashworth told us last season, about the politician who spent a lifetime campaigning for a particular reform, only to collapse into a profound melancholy once it was enacted? The loss of the struggle, you see, was far more tragic than the continuation of the grievance. He had nothing left to strive for, nothing left to hide.” Julian rose languidly, gliding towards a large, intricately carved screen draped with a heavy silk cloth, which stood in a shadowy corner of the studio. “But if you truly wish to understand me, Alaric, to truly console my artistic soul, then you must allow me to reveal something far more exquisite than mere suffering. You must learn to appreciate the perfect beauty of the unobserved, the utterly private masterpiece.”

Alaric’s gaze followed him, a flicker of apprehension in his eyes. “You speak in riddles, Julian. What on earth is behind that screen? Is it another of your satirical allegories, perhaps a rather pointed caricature of myself?” He forced a light laugh, but his tone held an edge of unease.

“My dear Alaric, do you truly imagine I would stoop to anything so crude, so painfully obvious?” Julian’s voice took on a sudden, chilling intensity. “No, this is something quite different. This is my true self, my unvarnished soul, transposed onto canvas. He reached out a hand towards the screen, then hesitated. “I am quite fond of Professor Devereaux, of course. But I know that you, Alaric, are better than he is. You cannot possibly have forgotten that you assured me most solemnly that nothing on earth would induce you to send it to any exhibition. You told Professor Devereaux precisely the same thing.” He stopped abruptly, and a strange, calculating gleam entered his eyes. He recalled Devereaux’s half-jesting remark during their last luncheon, “If you desire a truly bewildering fifteen minutes, get Alaric to explain why he insists on seeing your ‘unspeakable masterpiece.’ He attempted to enlighten me once, and it was a revelation of the most opaque kind.” Yes, perhaps Alaric, too, had his secrets, his hidden motives. He would try.

It was a face ravaged, distorted by some monstrous internal disease, a spiritual putrefaction made hideously manifest. The subtle curve of the lip, once so charmingly innocent, was now twisted into a sneer of unspeakable cruelty. A network of fine, cruel lines, etched by some invisible hand, spiderwebbed across the once flawless brow, lines born not of age, but of vice. The very texture of the paint seemed to have shifted, growing coarse and mottled in places, like diseased skin, while a ghastly smear of red, like fresh blood, tainted one corner of the mouth, as if a cruel deed had just been committed, staining the canvas itself.

Dorian watched him, a faint, almost imperceptible smile playing on his lips, a smile utterly devoid of warmth or humour. "No trick, Basil," he said, his voice soft, almost lyrical, yet chillingly calm. "No jest. No hand has touched it save yours, and mine, in the way one touches a living thing, a reflection of one’s very soul. For others, a deeper, more profound truth resides in the grotesque, in the decay that speaks of a life lived, however wickedly. But you, Basil, you created it. He remembered Lord Henry’s cynical pronouncements, Dorian’s youthful wish, a wish he had then dismissed as an idle fancy, a fleeting, poetic thought. Basil stared at him, his face ashen. His masterpiece, his proudest achievement, the culmination of his artistic vision, had become a horror, a grotesque mockery of its original beauty. His art, through some unholy alchemy, had become the very instrument of its revelation and preservation.

Does it not fill you with horror? Does it not compel you to change, to repent, to cleanse yourself of these monstrous deeds?" His voice rose, tinged with a desperate plea. "Think of what you have become! What you *are* becoming! This portrait, Dorian, it is your soul made visible! And it is damned!"

Dorian smiled again, a slow, cold spreading of his lips. "Horror, Basil? No, not horror. Curiosity, perhaps. A certain perverse fascination, undoubtedly. And an immense relief, I confess. For while it bears the scars, I remain as you see me now: young, unblemished, free. It suffers for me
